title: Financial Stability Report, No. 2 - 2026
summary: Banca d’Italia judges Italy’s domestic financial vulnerabilities moderate and little changed since spring. That conclusion rests on the condition of borrowers and intermediaries, even as the external environment has deteriorated. AI-related investment supported global output in the first half of 2026 and helped offset the energy shock from conflict in the Persian Gulf. The same investment creates an exposure for markets: prices embed considerable optimism about future earnings, long-term yields have risen, and some risk premiums remain compressed despite the recent correction in technology shares. A larger fall in US equities could therefore reach Italy even with relatively limited direct household exposure to US technology securities.

The Italian financial cycle was near neutral. Year-on-year GDP growth slowed to 0.8% in the third quarter as industry decelerated and net foreign demand subtracted from growth. Inflation eroded household purchasing power and saving capacity. Firms, in aggregate, retained ample liquidity and modest debt. These buffers leave room for considerable differences between borrowers. On the Bank’s baseline, financially vulnerable firms would account for just above 27% of corporate financial debt in 2027, down 1.4 percentage points. That share measures debt at firms meeting the vulnerability criteria, rather than projected losses to lenders. The stress comparison in Figure 1.18 makes both earnings and borrowing costs less favourable. Their joint movement matters in an energy shock.

The ten-year BTP–Bund spread had risen about 50 basis points from its January low while remaining below its twenty-year average. Secondary-market liquidity was still favourable. Bid–ask spreads were historically low, the market could absorb large orders, and trading volumes had returned to spring levels after a strong summer. Options nevertheless showed greater demand for protection against falling bond prices. The repo-market box on pp. 15–16 explains the potential connection: hedge funds can provide liquidity through relative-value trades, while financing positions against Italian sovereign collateral through a concentrated group of dealers, predominantly outside central clearing. A simultaneous withdrawal of financing could turn an apparently liquid trade into sales of bonds. The underlying data capture non-EU hedge funds only when a counterparty is in the EU.

Banks continued to report strong capitalisation and profitability and good credit quality. Aggregate resilience also depends on the institution and the portfolio. The mid-year CET1 ratio fell to 15.7% at significant Italian banks, while the ratio at less significant banks rose to 18.6%. The report examines supervisory expectations for provisioning legacy impaired exposures at smaller banks. The separate appendix gives loan stocks, coverage and guarantees, allowing readers to distinguish the protection against losses already recognised from the rate at which new problems emerge. The Bank kept its countercyclical buffer at zero in the third and fourth quarters. Its separate systemic risk buffer represented about €7.3 billion of common equity capital in June, reflecting a 1% requirement on relevant domestic exposures.

The assessment also covers risks outside banking. In an IVASS exercise based on end-2025 balance sheets, the Solvency II reform would release roughly €5 billion of capital and lift the solvency ratio by ten percentage points across a sample covering 83% of market assets. Firms have discretion over the released capital, so the estimated benefit does not establish demand for a particular asset. Italian alternative funds are largely closed-ended, limiting immediate redemption pressure. Links to foreign private credit nevertheless matter: foreign intermediaries provided more than four-fifths of the €15 billion lent to resident firms over three years. Incomplete information on exposures and financing limits the assessment of contagion. Finally, the Bank identifies concentration in service providers and the spread of frontier AI as operational risks that can affect several institutions at once. It draws no inference about the timing of a market correction from those vulnerabilities.

questions.question: How would a withdrawal of repo financing change the liquidity of long-dated BTPs?
questions.detail: The report documents concentration among dealers and hedge funds alongside strong cash-market depth. It cannot identify the price impact of a coordinated reduction in lending. For the size of a sovereign-spread position, seek SFTR breakdowns of repo maturity, haircut and clearing status alongside order-book depth and the cash–futures basis during comparable volatility episodes.

questions.question: Which Italian borrowers would transmit a second energy shock to bank capital?
questions.detail: The Bank’s microsimulation measures vulnerable firms’ share of debt and the appendix describes existing impaired loans. Neither number on its own gives lenders’ incremental losses. Compare sectoral energy exposure, repricing schedules, collateral recoveries and lender concentration in supervisory returns and bank disclosures. The result could change the ranking of bank credit exposures even if the aggregate ratio stays comfortable.

questions.question: How much of insurers’ regulatory headroom would support new risky assets?
questions.detail: The impact study estimates released capital using end-2025 positions. It does not show how management would deploy it or whether surrender risk would constrain deployment. For a view on demand for corporate bonds or private assets, consult IVASS solvency and liquidity data and firms’ investment plans. Separate changed accounting requirements from new purchasing capacity and actual purchases.
